To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a micromechanical parallel-class disk-array filter with an eighth-order bandpass response, an insertion loss of 0.16%, a bandwidth of 163 MHz, a termination impedance of 4 kOmega (or 2.7 times lower than a single disk), a 20 dB bandwidth of 290 MHz, and a shape factor of only about 1.78 has been designed and demonstrated.

a capacitively-transduced parallel-class disk-array filter can be realized that is 50% smaller than its single-disk resonator counterpart in terms of chip area, and has a termination impedance of 1/5 that of the single resonator.

a micromechanical parallel-class bandpass filter can be realized on a chip by using two capacitively-trans-duced disk-array sub-fil- ters in a parallel configuration, that this filter has a 163-Mhz eighth-order (i. e., four-pole, 0.16% bandwidth) bandpass response, that its insertion loss is 2.73 db, that its 20-dB shape factor is 1.78 (i. e., very sharp),
In summary, our research is concerned with
the realization of high-order, high-performance, low-impedance, and MSI micromechanically-cou- pled disk-array filters.
the development of high-performance micromechanically-based filters, and the demonstration of the feasibility of realizing a high-order filter response on a single chip.
the development of a high-performance micromechanical filter technology that is compatible with standard CMOS fabrication processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work represents the first demonstration of an on-chip MSI micromechanical bandpass filter with performance comparable to that of its macroscopic counterparts.
the filter of this work represents the highest-order, lowest-loss, and smallest termination-impedance micromechanical filter reported in the literature.

the filter presented here is a true MSI MEMS filter that has been realized on a single chip, is the first such filter to use capacitively-transduced composite resonators, and has the lowest termination impedance reported for any capacitively-transduced MEMS filter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
this is the first demonstration of a high-order micromechanical filter that combines a high quality factor (Q), a small termination impedance (R), and a low insertion loss.
we have successfully demonstrated a high-performance, high-frequency (i.e., 163 MHz), and high-order (i.e. eighth-order) filter response on a micromechanical chip.
this filter represents a major step toward the realization of high-performance, on-chip, high-order mechanical filters that are compatible with standard CMOS processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of capacitively-transferred micromechanical disk-array filters can enable the design of high-performance MSI mechanical filters with low-impedance outputs, which are not otherwise possible to implement with conventional single resonator-based micromechanical filter designs.

the use of multiple disk arrays in a single filter can provide a means to achieve the high-order filter response needed to realize a compact, high-frequency mechanical filter, while also allowing a reduction in termination impedance to facilitate the matching of other components.

the use of capacitively-transducted disk-array sub-filers allows for a reduction in termination impedance, which is the primary impediment for the use of capacitance-based transduction in MEMS filters.
